## FAQ | What am I expected to know *now*?

- Basic statistics: have a notion of probability, mean, median, and similar concepts.
- Familiarity with hypothesis testing and regression is a bonus.
- No prior coding experience is required.

## FAQ | What makes this course different from MKTG 401?

- We focus on **secondary data** instead of **primary data**.
- Secondary data is messy and comes from many different sources.
- This course is a data analysis deep dive: more code, more details, more technical.

## FAQ | What makes this course different from MSB 325?

- This a deeper dive into data analysis.
- Class is interactive.
- Many students find they learn more.

## FAQ | Why are we using R?

R is a free, open-source programming language for statistical computing, analysis, and data science.

- Largest repository of established and new statistical techniques.
- Friendly for non-programmers.
- A very active and helpful community.
- What you can *do* with R is in high demand.

## FAQ | My internship/job expects me to know Python. How do I learn it?

Python is also a general-purpose data analysis tool, it just isn't as *accessible* as R is. However, many jobs require you to know Python.

- Programming techniques and experience learned in R will make learning additional languages *much* easier.
- The BYU Statistics department has excellent courses to teach you Python.

## FAQ | Why Learn to Code If AI Can Do It?

- We are past asking, "Should I use AI?" The question is now, "When and how can I use AI?"
- Use AI to complement and accelerate your abilities and productivity, not to replace your effort and learning.
- Knowing how to code lets you read, test, and correct AI's work instead of blindly trusting it.

**You are still responsible for the analysis and the decisions it informs.**

## Deloitte | Verify the Evidence in Client Reports

**What happened (2025):** An AI-assisted report for Australia's government included nonexistent references and a fabricated court quotation. Deloitte corrected the report and repaid nearly **$98,000 of its $440,000 fee**.

**For marketers:** Verify the evidence behind market research, competitor claims, and campaign recommendations. Polished writing does not prove the evidence is real.

[Sources: Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/ab54858680ffc4ae6555b31c8fb987f3) and [refund reporting](https://psnews.com.au/government-urged-to-get-deloittes-total-fee-returned-for-delivering-a-botched-ai-report/167893/)

<div class="notes">

## FAQ | How do I study for a class like this?

1. Seek learning by study and faith (D&C 109:7).
2. Prepare for meetings by previewing material and coming with questions.
3. Actively code, take notes, and ask questions during meetings.
4. Practice coding by completing exercises and referencing supplementary material as needed.
5. Review exercise solutions and note where and why your work differs.
6. Use the knowledge checks to gauge how well you understand the material.
7. Work with classmates and utilize office hours.
8. Download and organize all materials, notes, and code.

## FAQ | What's the best way to learn how to code?

1. Learn by doing: Code during meetings and complete exercises.
2. Pay *careful* attention to details. READ SLOWLY.
3. Don't code from scratch. Start with previous work and solutions.
4. Look at and emulate good code.
5. Literally sketch what transformed data should look like in the end.
6. Use AI as a collaborator: ask for suggestions and explanations, not just solutions.

## FAQ | What role will generative AI play in this class?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is an important analytics tool, and employees may use it to understand and write code. Employees must also regulate their own use. [Early-stage research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.08872v1) suggests that active AI use may weaken learning during tasks such as writing or coding. We must balance the firm's productivity with each employee's intellectual and spiritual growth.

The gospel helps reconcile temporal and spiritual priorities. The following excerpt from ["Things as They Really Are 2.0"](https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/broadcasts/worldwide-devotional-for-young-adults/2024/11/13bednar?lang=eng) offers useful perspective:

## Remember to Work Toward What God Wants You to Become

"Now, I believe AI appropriately can assist in gathering information, critiquing our thinking, evaluating our writing style, and accelerating an iterative process of learning “line upon line [and] precept upon precept.” But the divine capacities to create and work belong uniquely to each of us as sons and daughters of God. We undoubtedly can generate and produce fabulous content for [school/church/work] with AI. But the objective is not merely producing or presenting impressive content; rather, it is working and becoming what God intends and yearns for us to become."

## Keep These Principles in Mind

- AI is a *tool*, neither good nor bad on its own. It can gather information and critique thinking, writing, or code, but it is not a source of truth and cannot replace personal revelation.
- Overreliance on AI can foster spiritual and temporal laziness. The work and learning process matters as much as the final product.
- AI cannot simulate or replace the influence of the Holy Ghost. Spiritual discernment remains essential.
- AI should supplement, not replace, human work, creativity, and divine capacities.

Remember - do not be "transformed from [employees] who can act into objects that are only acted upon."

## I Want You In Discovery Mode!

Our brains process the world in two ways:

- Discovery Mode: you are curious and explorative, eager to try things, learn, and take calculated risks.
- Defense Mode: you are cautious and protective, looking for threats whether real or imagined, and tend to avoid risks and retreat to safety.

Both are necessary - but only one is conducive to effectively learning programming and analytics.

[Get more information here.](https://www.catharticspacecounseling.com/blog/discover-mode-vs-defend-mode-how-your-brain-handles-anxiety) (not an endorsement of the services of Kristen Jacobsen)

## Identify | Specify the Managerial Problem and Evaluate Data

One of the most important skills you will gain over the course of the semester is the ability to recognize business pain points and translate them into specific and actionable analyses.

You will also learn how to synthesize data from multiple sources, and ask questions that can reasonably be answered based on the available data.

Good marketing analytics begins with asking the right questions and obtaining the right data.

## Cougar Tails | Identify the Planning Problem

**Hypothetical case:** BYU concessions wants to predict cougar tail demand for each home football game next season.

| Resource | Planning decision |
| :--- | :--- |
| Ingredients and packaging | How much should we order, and when? |
| Bakery staff and equipment time | How much time should each campus bakery reserve for cougar tails versus other baked goods? |
| Storage and delivery capacity | How much can we hold and move to the stadium? |

**Too few:** stockouts and missed sales. **Too many:** waste and less capacity for other products.

<div class="notes">

- This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a description of actual BYU concessions operations.
- The objective is a game-level unit forecast that informs ingredient orders and bakery scheduling across campus.
- In practice, collect stockout times, unsold inventory, and other-product demand. Observed sales can understate demand when supply runs out.
- All case figures and regression estimates come from Case-Study/build_cougar_tail_case.R, using ggplot2 for every chart, an R linear model, and a fixed random seed. No external records or assets were used.
- Assume no stockouts, so recorded sales approximate demand. This teaching assumption is retained in notes rather than on the slide.

</div>

## Import | Acquire the Needed Data

While primary data is gathered specifically to serve the research objectives at hand, secondary data was gathered for another purpose. Consult the original and most current source whenever possible and understand its context (i.e., use the **data dictionary**).

- Who collected it?
- Why was it collected?
- When was it collected?
- What was collected?
- How was it collected?

Acquiring secondary data may require interacting with databases, using APIs,  web scraping, etc.

## Cougar Tails | Import Game-Level Records

Join sales, schedules, weather, attendance, and pre-game ratings. **One row = one home game.**

<div class="case-data-table">

| Date | Week | Temp. (°F) | Attendance | BYU win % | Units sold | Sales ($) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2025-09-06 | 1 | 75 | 61,100 | 25 | 11,108 | 88,864 |
| 2025-09-20 | 3 | **NA** | 58,300 | 55 | 8,747 | 69,976 |
| 2025-10-04 | 5 | 74 | 58,800 | 55 | 8,258 | 66,064 |
| 2025-11-01 | 9 | 81 | 90,000 | 85 | 5,095 | 40,760 |
| 2025-11-15 | 11 | 45 | 58,300 | 85 | 10,091 | 80,728 |

</div>

- **NA** = missing.
- **BYU win %** = a pre-game estimate, not the game result.

<div class="notes">

- The complete synthetic schedule has six home games per season, in season weeks 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11: 60 games total.
- The raw import has 59 rows because the 2025 week-7 game was deliberately omitted. The other planted issues are a missing week-3 temperature and impossible week-9 attendance.
- Sales dollars equal units sold times the assumed constant $8 price. Dollars are an outcome, not a predictor of unit sales.
- The data generator also returns the fictional full schedule and verified source records used in the cleaning example.

</div>

## Tidy and Transform | Wrangle the Data

Secondary data can be **messy**. Data wrangling includes whatever tidying, cleaning, mutating, selecting, transforming, renaming, fusing, or filtering is needed to get the data into the needed form to summarize and model.

This can be *tedious*, but it is a vital analytics skill.

## Cougar Tails | Tidy and Check the Records

| Check | Problem in the raw import | Verify against source records |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Missing values | Week 3 temperature is NA | Retrieve game-time readings from a nearby weather station's historical archive. |
| Schedule coverage | Week 7 game is absent | Match the athletics season schedule to concessions' point-of-sale exports; retrieve the missing game's transactions. |
| Reasonable values | Week 9 attendance is 90,000 | Check the stadium's seating capacity and verify attendance against ticket-scan records. |

<div class="notes">

- The 64,000 capacity is an exercise assumption, not a claim about LaVell Edwards Stadium's current capacity.
- Cross-reference the full season schedule with the sales data using a unique season/game key. A missing row is different from a game with zero sales.
- If a source cannot resolve a missing or impossible value, flag it and document the chosen treatment; do not silently invent a replacement.
- The fictional recovered October 18 record has week 7, temperature 80°F, attendance 59,600, pre-game BYU win probability 25%, 10,411 units, and $83,288 sales.
- The missing temperature is 90°F; corrected week-9 attendance is 49,900. After repairs, there are 60 complete records. In a real project, obtain these values from the sources described in the table rather than assume them.
- Check revenue = units × $8 under this exercise's fixed-price assumption. These repairs restore the same complete records used for all charts and the regression.

</div>

## Cougar Tails | Transform a Pre-Game Rating

Turn the estimated BYU win probability into an **opponent difficulty** category:

| Estimated chance BYU wins | Difficulty | Example from the imported records |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 70% or higher | Low | 85% → Low |
| 40% to less than 70% | Medium | 55% → Medium |
| Less than 40% | High | 25% → High |

## Visualize | Summarize the Data

Summarizing data is initially about discovery. It includes computing **statistics** (i.e., numerical summaries) and creating **data visualizations** (i.e., graphical summaries).

- Summarizing data is closely tied with data wrangling.
- Summarizing data is often not an end in itself.

## Cougar Tails | Explore Temperature and Sales

Warmer games tend to have lower sales, with plenty of variation.

<img src="Figures/cougar_tail_temperature.png" alt="Scatter plot of 60 hypothetical games, showing a noisy negative association between game temperature and cougar tails sold." width="900" />
</div>

## Cougar Tails | Compare Opponent Difficulty

Average sales are higher against tougher opponents.

<div class="case-chart">
<img src="Figures/cougar_tail_opponent.png" alt="Bar chart of mean unit sales: Low difficulty 8,254 across 26 games; Medium 8,574 across 20 games; High 10,967 across 14 games." width="900" />
</div>

<p class="case-caption">Hypothetical data; averages across all 60 games. Other game characteristics differ across groups too.</p>

## Cougar Tails | Look for a Seasonal Pattern

Sales tend to decline across the season, with ups and downs.

<div class="case-chart">
<img src="Figures/cougar_tail_season_week.png" alt="Line chart of sales averaged across 10 seasons at each season week: 9,733, 10,197, 9,059, 9,252, 7,594, and 8,125 units in weeks 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11." width="900" />
</div>

<p class="case-caption">Hypothetical data; each point averages the same season week across 10 seasons (10 games per point).</p>

<div class="notes">

- Align games by week within the season, then average across seasons. A single average for each calendar year would answer a different question.
- The six week averages are 9,733.0; 10,196.6; 9,059.0; 9,252.4; 7,594.4; and 8,125.1 units.
- The irregular line is intentional. Temperature, opponents, attendance, and unmeasured factors vary across games; this is not a causal estimate of the passage of time.

</div>

## Model | Inference and Prediction

Models *extract information* from the data to inform our managerial decision.

- In order to inform the marketing mix, the models we use are often inferential.
- Some managerial decisions only rely on prediction.

## Cougar Tails | Model Sales Together

**Outcome: cougar tails sold per game.**

<div class="case-equation">

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Sales}_i ={}& \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{Week}_i \\
&+ \beta_2\text{Medium}_i + \beta_3\text{High}_i \\
&+ \beta_4\text{Temperature}_i + \beta_5\text{Attendance}_i + \varepsilon_i
\end{aligned}
$$

</div>

- **Week, temperature (°F), and attendance (people)** enter as continuous variables.
- **Medium** and **High** are 0/1 indicators; **Low** is the reference category.
- Each row is a game; the error term captures unexplained variation.

## Cougar Tails | Read the Model Results

**Linear regression of unit sales.**

<div class="case-model-table">

| Model term | Estimate (units) | Standard error |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Intercept | 8,250 | 2,492 |
| Season week: 1 week later | −270 | 39 |
| Medium difficulty vs. Low | +776 | 282 |
| High difficulty vs. Low | +2,292 | 340 |
| Temperature: 1°F warmer | −94.77 | 9.61 |
| Attendance: 1 more person | +0.150 | 0.046 |

</div>

<div class="notes">

- The displayed coefficients and standard errors are rounded from an actual OLS fit to the same synthetic data shown earlier; they are not independently invented table entries.
- Formula: units ~ season_week + difficulty + temperature_f + attendance. Temperature and attendance are unbinned numeric variables in their original units; Low difficulty is the reference category, not an equally spaced numeric rating.
- The intercept is the fitted value at week 0, temperature 0°F, attendance 0, and Low difficulty. That combination is outside the observed range; use the full equation for realistic games, not the intercept on its own.
- Each coefficient is an association holding the other included predictors constant, not a causal effect. In-sample R-squared is 0.788, not a forecast accuracy score.
- The date is represented by season week. The win-probability estimate is represented by the difficulty categories. Revenue is deliberately excluded because it is calculated directly from units sold.
- In real forecasting, use the known schedule and pre-game difficulty estimates plus forecast temperature and expected attendance, not future actual observations. Revisit forecasts as game day approaches.
- Standard errors are conventional OLS standard errors for illustration. This toy model is not validated for real BYU decisions; use a held-out season to assess prediction error and uncertainty before relying on it.

</div>

## Communicate | Report and Create Data Products

Effectively communicating marketing insights brings us full circle and highlights the necessity of domain expertise.

The analyst needs to **interpret results in a way that clearly informs the managerial decision**. You may hear this referred to as "storytelling."

## Cougar Tails | Communicate the Findings

**In this hypothetical dataset:**

- Warmer temperatures and later season weeks are **associated with lower sales**.
- Tougher opponents and larger crowds are **associated with higher sales** in the fitted model.
- The patterns may help forecast demand; they do **not** show that changing temperature or opponents would cause sales to change.

Use game-level forecasts to plan ingredient orders and bakery time, with a buffer for uncertainty and room for other baked goods.

## Cougar Tails | Brief Concessions Managers

**Upcoming game:** Week 3, High difficulty, 70°F, 60,000 attendees.

| Planning measure | Takeaway |
| :--- | :--- |
| Expected sales | About **12,100 tails** |
| 80% model prediction interval | About **10,800–13,300 tails** |
| Production target | **13,300 tails** |

Reserve inventory and production capacity for the target. Update the plan as weather and attendance forecasts change.

We use the upper interval amount to balance the risk of missed sales against waste; it is not a guarantee that we won't sell out.

<div class="notes">

- All scenario inputs are teaching assumptions. The model fitted to all 60 synthetic games predicts 12,079 units, with an 80% OLS prediction interval of 10,827–13,331 units for a single upcoming game.
- The displayed forecast and interval are rounded to the nearest hundred. The production target uses the upper prediction limit with the same rounding: round(13,331 / 100) × 100 = 13,300.
- Choosing the upper interval amount is a management decision, not a statistically optimized inventory policy. The model prediction interval is conditional on the supplied predictor values and does not include uncertainty in future weather or attendance inputs.
- The case assumes no historical stockouts. Actual forecasting would also need stockout records and evaluation across more held-out seasons.

</div>

## Cougar Tails | Brief Bakery and Purchasing

Assume each baker can produce **1,200 tails** in a 12-hour window. We need **12 bakers**: 11 can produce only 13,200.

| Production assignment | Staff allocation |
| :--- | ---: |
| Cougar tails | 12 bakers |
| Mint brownies | 2 additional production staff |
| Kettle corn | 2 additional production staff |
| **Total** | **16 people** |

Stage ingredients for **133 batches of 100 tails** and 13,300 sleeves.

<div class="notes">

- Production rates, staffing, batch size, and packaging requirements are assumptions for the classroom case, not verified BYU operating standards.
- Required cougar-tail bakers = ceiling(13,300 / 1,200) = 12. Their combined capacity is 14,400, but the production target remains 13,300 rather than automatically using all capacity.
- The 1,200-tail capacity is each baker's total contribution within the 12-hour production window, not a requirement for a continuous 12-hour shift; schedule breaks and coverage within that capacity assumption.
- The staffing plan reserves two additional people for mint brownies and two for kettle corn, for 16 total. These other-product allocations are planning assumptions, not outputs of the cougar-tail model.
- Ingredients come from the recipe bill of materials for 133 batches of 100 tails. Check on-hand usable ingredients, packaging, supplier lead times, equipment capacity, storage, and delivery before committing the schedule across campus bakeries.

</div>

## Cougar Tails | Brief the Analytics Team

- **Temperature:** 1°F warmer is associated with about **95 fewer units**, holding the other included predictors constant.
- **Attendance:** 1,000 more people is associated with about **150 more units**, under the same adjustment.

| 2025 holdout: 6 games | Mean absolute error |
| :--- | ---: |
| Regression trained on 2016–2024 | **671 tails per game** |
| Always predict the training-set mean | **1,585 tails per game** |

The model improves on this simple baseline. Monitor forecast error by game.

<div class="notes">

- Validation uses a separate fit on 54 games from 2016–2024 and tests on six games from 2025. Neither the coefficients nor the baseline mean use holdout outcomes.
- After validation, the presentation's coefficient table and upcoming-game forecast use a refit on all 60 records. Both sets of results are calculated by Case-Study/build_cougar_tail_case.R.
- These are retrospective predictions using observed weather and attendance; operational evaluation should use the forecasts available when ingredient and staffing decisions are made.
- One six-game holdout is not enough to establish operational reliability. Check multiple held-out seasons, prediction-interval coverage, and whether stockouts censor demand before deployment.

</div>
